To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
BAPTA interacts with lipid monolayers in a Ca2+- and lipid-dependent manner.
BAPTA is able to bind to the plasma membrane in a Ca2+- and lipid-dependent manner.
the chelator BAPTA interacts with phospholipides and that this interaction is Ca2+‐sensitive and may contribute to the chelation of Ca2+ ions close to the membrane.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of new tools for Ca2+‐imaging and Ca2+‐sensing.
the molecular mechanisms that control calcium‐dependent signaling triggered by calcium entry via voltage‐gated calcium channels.
the study of the molecular basis of the Ca2+/calmodulin‐dependent inhibition of CaV2.2 Ca channels.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
BAPTA is a Ca2+ chaperone that can interact with phospholipides and that is able to modulate the activity of Ca2+ channels.
the BAPTA‐induced inhibition is not due to a Ca2+ sequestration by the chelator but to its interaction with the phospholipids of the oocyte membrane.
, in addition to the well‐known ability of BAPTAs to chelate and sequestrate Ca2+, these molecules are able to interact in a Ca2+/lipid‐dependent manner with the membrane.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
Ca2+‐chelating agents are not only chelators, they are also lipid‐modulating compounds.
the Ca2+ cheler BAPTA is a phospholipid‐like molecule.
BAPTA is a Ca2+ chaperone that is able to chelate the Ca2+ ions released by voltage‐gating of CaV2.
The main takeaway from our work is that
BAPTA is not only a good chelator but also a good Ca2+‐sensitive probe.
the ability to interact with lipids should be considered in the future as a new property of Ca2+ chaperone molecules.
the ability of BAPTAs to interact with lipids may be a general property of this class of Ca2+‐chelating molecules.
